titre: Angkor Wat Isn't a Lone Temple: Lidar Revealed an Entire City
accroche: A 2012 laser survey saw through the forest around Angkor Wat. Underneath: hundreds of ponds and an urban grid no one had ever mapped.
contenu_vulgarise:
To most visitors, Angkor Wat is a temple: stone towers, bas-reliefs, a vast rectangular moat all around. That's also what the site's first cartographers thought, in the early twentieth century, stopping their surveys at the temple's enclosure and its moat. Behind that enclosure, though, the Cambodian forest was hiding an entire city, and it took an airborne laser to bring it into view.

## A Laser That Sees Through the Trees

In 2012, an international team gathered in the Khmer Archaeology LiDAR Consortium, including archaeologist Damian Evans, flies a laser remote-sensing instrument over the heart of Greater Angkor, covering 370 square kilometers. The principle behind lidar is simple: the instrument fires millions of laser pulses at the ground and measures how long each one takes to bounce back. Some beams pass through gaps in the foliage and bounce off the ground or the remains buried beneath it. By keeping only the lowest returns, researchers reconstruct a model of the terrain stripped of its vegetation, revealing features just a few centimeters high that are invisible from the ground.

Beneath the forest cover, the image reveals an urban grid around Angkor Wat made of blocks roughly a hundred meters on a side, each containing residential mounds and ponds: somewhere between 250 and 300 ponds counted around the temple itself, and 125 to 130 around the neighboring temple of Ta Prohm, according to the paper published by Evans and archaeologist Roland Fletcher in the journal Antiquity in 2015. The authors cautiously estimate a resident population of around 4,500 people in the immediate vicinity of Angkor Wat, a maintenance workforce of about 25,000, and a support population exceeding 125,000.

## The End of the "Compact Temple"

An archaeological map published in 2007 by Evans and a French-Australian-Cambodian team, based on an earlier airborne radar survey and decades of ground surveys, had already placed the Greater Angkor settlement over nearly 3,000 square kilometers, with a water-management network of reservoirs and canals exceeding 1,000 square kilometers: enough, in the authors' own words, to make it "the most extensive urban complex of the preindustrial world," far larger than Tikal, the largest fully surveyed Maya city, at roughly one hundred to one hundred fifty square kilometers. The 2012 lidar survey refines this map all the way to the heart of the Angkor Wat temple itself, right where earlier surveys thought there was only an enclosure and a moat. Evans and Fletcher state it plainly: the model of a compact "temple city" bounded by its walls is no longer compatible with what the data show.

## What This Survey Shifts

Angkor Wat, then, was never an exception set down in the jungle: it's the dense core of a settlement that spread far beyond its moats, with its own residential quarters and its own water reserves. What the earliest surveys took for the edges of the site were only the edges of what could be seen through the trees.

repere.texte: The archaeological map of Greater Angkor published in 2007 covers 2,848 square kilometers and describes a water-management network exceeding 1,000 square kilometers: enough, according to its authors, to make it "the most extensive urban complex of the preindustrial world," far larger than Tikal (100 to 150 square kilometers), the largest fully surveyed Maya city.
repere.source: Evans, Pottier, Fletcher et al., Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2007

carte.punch: The 2012 lidar survey revealed that Angkor Wat wasn't a lone temple, but the core of an entire city.
carte.idee: In 2012, a laser survey saw through the forest around Angkor Wat. Underneath: an urban grid of hundreds of ponds and residential quarters that ground surveys had never seen. The compact "temple city" model is no longer compatible with this map, according to Evans and Fletcher.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: The landscape of Angkor Wat redefined, Antiquity (Cambridge Core)
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The full 2015 paper, with lidar maps overlaid on historical surveys dating back to 1909.

quiz.question: What did the 2012 laser survey (lidar) reveal beneath the forest surrounding Angkor Wat?
choix: An urban grid of residential blocks and hundreds of ponds, extending well beyond the temple's moat
A second temple, identical to Angkor Wat, buried underground
A canal system predating the temple's construction, since abandoned
The foundations of a second, older enclosure wall than the one visible today
quiz.explication: Lidar revealed, beneath the forest cover, a grid of blocks roughly a hundred meters on a side containing residential mounds and ponds (250 to 300 at Angkor Wat), showing that the temple is the core of an urban area far larger than its enclosure.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does a lidar instrument manage to map the ground beneath dense forest?
choix: It measures heat radiating from the ground, which trees don't block
It fires laser pulses, some of which pass through gaps in the foliage and bounce off the ground, and these are isolated from the other returns
It combines several aerial photographs taken from different angles
It analyzes variations in Earth's magnetic field beneath the canopy
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Lidar fires millions of laser pulses; some reach the ground through gaps in the foliage. By keeping only the lowest returns, researchers reconstruct a model of the terrain stripped of vegetation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the map published by Evans and colleagues in 2007, how does Greater Angkor compare to other fully surveyed preindustrial cities?
choix: It is markedly smaller than Tikal, the largest known Maya city
It is comparable to Tikal, both covering around 150 square kilometers
It is the most extensive preindustrial urban complex known, far larger than Tikal
No comparison is possible, since Tikal has never been mapped
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The authors describe Greater Angkor as the most extensive preindustrial urban complex known, covering roughly 900 to 1,000 square kilometers, compared with 100 to 150 square kilometers for Tikal, the largest fully surveyed Maya city.
